- Latency SLO: P95 < 350ms for short requests; < 800ms for the long-context path is acceptable
- Data: PHI, so Private/Dedicated preference and auditability matter

Sara — thanks for the clear data. Quick reply while I loop in Dev and Rishi for ops sizing and cost knobs. High-level guidance up front:

- H100: best for the long-context 24k token sessions (largest model footprints + KV cache headroom). Fewer cards needed for long sessions but highest per-card committed cost. Good for predictable latency under sustained long queries.
- A100: middle ground. Better than older cards on throughput but you still hit memory limits with 24k dense KV caches unless you shard aggressively. Good if you can split the long path or accept slightly higher retrieval and recompute.
- L4: cost-efficient and excellent for short-context, low-memory inference. Not suitable as the sole platform for your 24k sessions because of constrained cache/memory. Best used as the majority lane for short requests with fallthrough to H100 pool for long sessions.

I'll ask Dev to sketch a concrete committed mix and Rishi to include an ops fallthrough policy (bursting/buffer) and estimated committed monthly cost.

—Olga

Team — I modeled a conservative Dedicated footprint that balances memory safety for long sessions and unit cost for the short path. Notes and assumptions are inline; I also updated KiteHealth_GPU_fitment_v2.xlsx and attached to this thread.

Assumptions:
- Long sessions (24k tokens) consume ~3.5x KV memory compared to 4k baseline on our internal tests (model-dependent).
- Average short-session token length: 300 tokens.
- Target average GPU utilization target for committed pool: 65–70% (headroom for spikes).

Proposed committed mix (candidate):
- H100 pool: 8x H100 (pinned for long-context model variants) — primary for long-path sessions and model variants that require FP8 precision or large KV caches.
- A100 pool: 16x A100 (general-purpose medium-context fallback) — handles medium-long requests and offers better cost per token than H100 for batchy workloads.
- L4 pool: 48x L4 (short-path, high-concurrency cheap lane) — covers ~80% of short requests and offloads tail from H100/A100.

Operational fallthrough: 
- Route by request classifier: short requests -> L4; medium -> A100; long -> H100.
- If H100 capacity saturated, overflow to A100 with degraded latency and optional prefix-recompute (acceptable within +200ms tail).
- Autoscale/burst: configure burst capacity to spin up additional A100 or H100 on demand (reserve burst credits in contract).

Estimated committed monthly cost (ballpark, committed discounts applied):
- H100 x8: ~$120k/month
- A100 x16: ~$64k/month
- L4 x48: ~$28k/month
- Total committed: ~$212k/month (excludes network/storage & added support tiers).

Risks & mitigations:
- OOM risk on A100 for long sessions — guard with KV sharding and model truncation; prefer keeping long sessions on H100.
- Cost sensitivity — L4 mix can be increased if long-session volume stays low; conversely, if long paths grow, convert some A100 to H100 in later quarters.

I attached a quick sensitivity tab in the spreadsheet that shows token/hour mix breakpoints where swapping 4x A100 -> 1x H100 becomes cost justified.

—Dev

Sara / KiteHealth procurement — tagging onto Dev and Olga's proposal with the recommended rollout and contract notes.

Rollout suggestion:
1) Phase 1 (pilot, 6 weeks): commit to the L4-heavy baseline (24 L4) + 2x H100 seed for long-path safety. Validate classification accuracy and hit rates for long-path overflow.
2) Phase 2 (production commit): move to the candidate committed mix (H100 x8 / A100 x16 / L4 x48) once long-path hit rate justifies H100 capacity. Include an A/B window for 30 days where we collect QoS & cost telemetry and allow a one-time sku adjustment.

Contract items to request from Procurement:
- Burst credits: define monthly burst budget to allow autoscale A100->H100 during predictable spikes without immediate overage invoices.
- SLA exceptions: agreed fallback to A100 with documented latency degradation envelope and sample failure modes (OOM handling).
- Audit items: ensure log retention and key management meet your compliance needs (we can surface SOC2 artifacts).
